summary: Defines an address allocation policy that encodes the address of the Rendezvous Point (RP) inside an IPv6 multicast group address. For PIM Sparse Mode, this works as a group-to-RP mapping mechanism and simplifies multicast configuration across domains.

eli5.summary: The meeting place for a group is written right into the group's address, as if a party invitation had the street address built into its name.

questions: how does embedded rp work in ipv6 multicast
what is the riid field in an ipv6 multicast address
subtitle: Hiding the multicast rendezvous point's address inside the IPv6 group address itself.

tldr.problem: Inter-domain Any Source Multicast on IPv6 had no way to share information about active sources between domains, because MSDP was deliberately not specified for IPv6, and SSM alone was not expected to be enough in the short term.
tldr.mechanism: A new flag bit (R) in the IPv6 multicast address marks an address that carries the RP's address: the RP's network prefix, its length and a 4-bit interface ID are encoded in the group address, and PIM-SM routers derive the RP from it.
tldr.outcome: Routers need no multicast configuration except the RP itself, and neither MSDP nor BSR is needed. The RFC updates RFC 3306 and is itself updated by RFC 7371.

today: RFC 3956 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 3306, and it is itself updated by RFC 7371. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: The Problem and the Idea
sections.content:
In PIM Sparse Mode (PIM-SM), traffic for a group meets at a Rendezvous Point (RP). On IPv4, RPs in different domains tell each other about active sources using MSDP. MSDP was deliberately not specified for IPv6, which makes inter-domain Any Source Multicast (ASM) unusable. Source-Specific Multicast (SSM) avoids the problem but is not a complete solution, and the RFC notes it seems unlikely that SSM could be the only inter-domain mechanism in the short term.

This RFC defines an address allocation policy in which the RP's address is encoded in the IPv6 multicast group address, plus a PIM-SM group-to-RP mapping that uses it. Such addresses are called embedded-RP addresses. The scheme builds on unicast-prefix-based multicast addresses (RFC 3306) and updates that RFC's address format.

Beyond inter-domain ASM, the RFC says it also serves intra-domain ASM with scoped addresses, and can replace the Bootstrap Router protocol (BSR) for automatic RP discovery. Routers need no multicast configuration unless they act as an RP.
sections.eli5: Normally every router has to be told where the group's meeting place is. Here the group's name already says where the meeting place is, so nobody has to be told.

sections.title: The Modified Address Format
sections.content:
The base format from RFC 3306 is: 8 bits of 11111111, 4 flag bits, 4 scope bits, 8 reserved bits, an 8-bit plen, a 64-bit network prefix and a 32-bit group ID. This RFC takes the second high-order flag bit as the R-bit and splits the reserved field into 4 reserved bits and a 4-bit RIID (RP interface ID). The flags read 0RPT.

When the highest-order flag bit is 0 and R is 1, the address embeds an RP address. Then P MUST be 1, and so T MUST be 1, which gives the prefix FF70::/12. When R is 0, the address follows the older semantics, and RIID MUST be sent as zero and ignored on receipt.

Behavior is unspecified if P or T is not 1. The range FFF0::/12, where the two high-order flag bits are 11, is intentionally left unspecified, and implementations SHOULD NOT treat it as Embedded-RP without further IETF specification.
sections.eli5: One tiny switch in the address says 'the meeting place is hidden in here'. A few extra bits then say which door of the meeting place to use.

sections.title: Extracting the RP Address
sections.content:
Only unicast-prefix-based ASM addresses can embed an RP. To be processed, an address must be in FF70::/12, must have plen not equal to 0 (zero would mean SSM) and must have plen no greater than 64, since larger values would overlap the group ID.

The RP address is derived in two steps. First, copy the first plen bits of the network prefix into a zeroed 128-bit address. Second, replace the last 4 bits with the RIID.

Routers MUST apply at least the same validity checks to the derived address as to an RP learned by other means such as BSR or MSDP, and at least fe80::/10, ::/16 and ff00::/8 MUST be excluded. This matters because the information comes from an untrusted source: any Internet user.

Because RIID 0 is reserved, one combination of scope, prefix and group ID can have up to 2^4-1 = 15 RPs, but each such address is its own group, so there is only one RP per multicast address. The non-significant prefix bits need not be zero in some deployments, which lets group allocations follow unicast prefix allocations.
sections.eli5: To find the meeting place, take the street part of the address, fill the rest with zeros, and put the door number on the end.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
The RFC gives four examples for a network administrator holding 2001:DB8::/32.

  • Example 1: the RP sits on subnet 2001:DB8:BEEF:FEED::/64. Groups look like FF7x:y40:2001:DB8:BEEF:FEED::/96 and the RP is 2001:DB8:BEEF:FEED::y, leaving 32 bits of group IDs.
  • Example 2: using plen=32, groups come from FF7x:y20:2001:DB8::/64 and the RP is 2001:DB8::y, a loopback address injected into routing. This leaves 64 bits for group IDs.
  • Example 3: customers get prefixes like FF7x:y20:2001:DB8:DEAD::/80, but the RP is still 2001:DB8::y, because plen counts only the first 32 bits of the network prefix.
  • Example 4: an organization wanting its own PIM-SM domain uses FF7x:y30:2001:DB8:BEEF::/80, giving RP 2001:DB8:BEEF::y.

Here x is the scope and y is the RP's interface ID.
sections.eli5: Four sample invitations show different ways to write the meeting place into the name, depending on how big a neighbourhood you control.

sections.title: Running RPs
sections.content:
Redundancy: because the RP address is tied to the group address, usual failover tools such as BSR or Anycast-RP with MSDP cannot be used as-is. Anycast RP using PIM, or anycasting the RP address in the IGP, are the most feasible options; they are outside this memo's scope.

Deployment: with no inter-domain MSDP state, each Designated Router (DR) next to major sources could act as an RP. If that DR fails, the transmission may not work anyway. Different groups can map to different RPs to share load.

Addressing: an RP can have any unicast prefix up to /64, with the interface identifier set by hand to match RIID. RIID 0 must not be used because it would clash with the Subnet-Router Anycast address. With embedded-RP, BSR or other RP configuration is not needed across the PIM domain.

Control: MSDP source and group filtering does not stop outsiders who guess a group address, so real protection needs PIM scoping borders. Embedded-RP gives roughly the same default protection as MSDP with SA filtering. A new issue is that outsiders can register with or join to an RP; the RP can filter which groups it allows.
sections.eli5: Because the meeting place is in the group's name, you cannot easily move it. Operators choose where to put it and who may use it.

sections.title: Group-to-RP Mapping in PIM-SM
sections.content:
The only PIM-SM change is to add this as one more group-to-RP mapping method. The derived RP is used for Reverse Path Forwarding lookups, for Join/Prune processing and for Register-encapsulation. For addresses in FF70::/12, the embedded-RP mapping MUST be treated as the longest possible match and as higher priority than any other mechanism, to avoid loops and inconsistencies.

Unlike other mappings, which can be precomputed, this one must be recomputed for each new group address mapping to a different RP; results may be cached. Support is needed in the RP, the DR next to the senders, and any router on the path from any receiver to the RP. Shortest Path Tree formation and Register-Stop use (S,G) Joins and need no support.

The non-normative overview: a receiver learns a group address, sends an MLD Report, and its DR starts the PIM-SM Join towards the encoded RP, whether local or remote. A sender's DR sends the packets unicast-encapsulated in Register messages to the encoded RP. All messages follow PIM-SM; only how the RP is found differs.
sections.eli5: Routers read the meeting place from the group's name, then do everything else the usual way.

sections.title: Scalability
sections.content:
The embedded-RP inter-domain model behaves as if every group formed its own Internet-wide PIM domain, with a single RP per group wherever receivers and senders are. The result is a flat, RP-centered topology. Foreign sources now send unicast-encapsulated data to the foreign RP responsible for the group, which matters for large groups with many heavy senders.

The Internet-wide MSDP state of IPv4 ASM is eliminated. Backbone routers may hold (*,G) and (S,G,rpt) state between receivers and the RP, plus (S,G) state if the shortest path tree is used, but the RFC concludes the total state is smaller.

A drawback is that users indirectly pick the RP, so it may not exist or be reachable; the RFC says this is relatively significant but not very different from today, since MLDv2 (S,G) joins have the same result. An advantage is that every group has a responsible RP that can control, to some extent, who sends to the group.
sections.eli5: Every group gets its own single meeting place, so there is less news to pass between cities, but a meeting place can be missing or overloaded.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
RP addresses are now visible in group addresses, so they are easier to spot as single points of failure and may attract other attacks. Operators are encouraged to secure these routers. Any RP must accept PIM-SM Join, Prune and Register messages from any DR, which creates a possible denial-of-service risk. The RP can discard such messages for all addresses that do not encode its own address.

Implementations SHOULD allow manual configuration of which multicast prefixes may be used, which can limit an RP to designated groups. Routers supporting this specification are RECOMMENDED not to act as RPs unless explicitly configured, since becoming an RP needs no advertisement.

The embedded-RP threat model is similar to SSM: both greatly reduce threats on the sender side. The derived RP address MUST pass at least the same validity checks as any other, excluding at least fe80::/10, ::/16 and ff00::/8.
sections.eli5: Since the meeting place is public, bad guys can find it too, so it should be locked down and told which groups it may host.

fields.name: flgs
fields.desc: Flags 0RPT; R=1, P=1, T=1 gives FF70::/12.

fields.name: RIID
fields.desc: RP interface ID; replaces the last 4 bits of the RP address.

fields.name: plen
fields.desc: Bits of network prefix used for the RP; 1 to 64.
